blocks.x: How's everything going?
Fine, fine.
We're recording this afternoon. This is September the 1st, 1959 at 818 St. Peter Street. And this is Dick Allen talking.
Mack Fairhurst and Prince Miller.
We're going to play Punch some of his records so he can tell us what's what about him.

This is a tiny firearm here Punch known as Blue Moon Blues. Now the other side is doing the Jug Jug. There's no personnel listed here. In some of the records it just says that you're featured. Now I'm just trying to see if you...
I played there a good while for him.
Joe McDonald? Yeah.

Now I tell you another fella I forgot about. I was making a record. He didn't make no. You might have heard of him, but I wasn't in a long time. Sir Oliver Bibbs. Sir Oliver Bibbs. Yeah, that's where he'd give his name. I waited with him in Chicago at the club silhouette. I waited at the Gehrig Ball. I waited in Springfield with him at the club. Did he have a band? Yeah, he owned a band. Sir Oliver Bibbs.
What instrument did he play?
Drums.
You left Chicago in 1945, you were saying. 49. 49. 49.
When did you go to...

. I must be moving blood on some on it. Gerald Rays. Hey. Excuse me Bill. What was that? I forget what it was. Look it up. Now the first thing he put out there is this. Johnny Johnson, all of us called him in the country. We all was together. We all called him Rooster. Everybody called Johnny Don Rooster. When he see that he gone home. No. Must have been somebody like me told about it. Now me and them boys all of them down by the foot of the time something. Made out of living out of it. When we young kids. That's Ruby. Must have been blue on the firehouse. Blue?
Blue. William Blue. Fountain Blue they called. Blue. Blue. Blue. William Blue. Fountain Blue they called. dear
Just about them make it, didn't they?
River Blues, that's a contingent out of the Missourians.

Yeah, I think so. Let me ask you something. You and Lonnie work where now? R-A-C-E-L-E-N-D. Raceland? Yeah. Where's that at? It's about 40 miles from there. Louisiana. Yeah. You played together for how long? I'd say about three years. We were young kids. Just the two of you? Yes, just the two of you. We didn't have no band. Where would you play? Well, them old numbers. Remember them old tunes I'd sing to you, Dick?
Mm-hmm.

Old numbers. Beautiful doll. And Take Your Hands Away. And Blues. A whole lot of blues, you know. A lot of blues. Oh, he was a fine guitar, man. He's the guitar on this, I think. Yeah, but the only thing. Did you ever hear of Blind Willie Dunn? Yeah, I heard him. Was he Ed Lang? I don't know.
Where did you hear Blind Willie Dunn?

I heard his records. Oh, yeah. Well, you know, Lonnie Johnson played guitar with Blind Willie Dunn, and some of them are reported to have... They have two guitars. Yeah. It's been reported that King Oliver played on one of the records. To me, it didn't sound like it. How about you? Did it sound like it to you?
Well, that's what Johnny Wiggs says, and he heard Oliver in person. He said he was just playing his old style that he played before he went to normal.

Oh. Mm-hmm. Well... Lonnie never makes records with Lonnie because he left here way before me. Did you ever see him? Did you ever run across him after he'd become better known in yourself? Did you? Did you ever get together together? Yeah, I never really did. Did you ever play with anybody? Did you ever play in the same group together? Well, I'm going to tell you what happened. I was with a big show named Bronze Manigans. Yeah. And we played in Cleveland, Ohio. And they hired him there to do specials with the guitar. Yeah. And he come out and did an act now. Listen. Yeah. Didn't play in the band. Come out and did an act with us on guitar. Mm-hmm. And sung his song. That's where I first heard that thing he made about... What that thing was? Oh, shit. See, I can't think of anything. That thing always on my mind. Tomorrow. Tomorrow. Yeah. The record he made. Mm-hmm. All right. Let's see what else I can think of now.
I want to quiz him.
Yeah, go ahead.
What was Joe Howard?

Joe Howard used to be a trumpet player, but tell me he got on bass. But I can say this. Before I left here, Joe Howard showed me a whole lot of stuff on trumpet. And gave me a whole lot of musical ideas. He was a mighty fine man, boy. And to tell me he plays tuba now, I don't know. He's dead. Since I've been back. Why does he live? I want to. He's dead. He's dead. No, I didn't know that. I didn't know that.
Well, did you ever work with Old Man Allen's brass band?
No. Did you know Henry Allen? Sure. Did you ever play with Henry Allen? No. Did you know Higginbottom? Sure. Did you ever play with Higginbottom?
What about down here, Punch? When you got down? No.

I'm going to tell him something first. Red Allen named his daddy. Henry Allen. That's right. All right. Now, as you talk about the old man and the young one. The young one. The young one? Yeah. No. But I tell you what I did. I taught him a whole lot. You taught Red Allen a lot? I taught Red Allen a whole lot. I know Red Allen very well. Well, he's a younger kid now. I mean, I believe he looked old, but he's a young fella. Taught Red Allen. All right. That's fine. There was a kid in him at the Garrick Bar in Chicago. There were two bands. I was a son of a big, but Red Allen was there with a band. Well, this band, I guess. And he told the boys to ask me, was he an old man? You know, how old he was about. So, I told him. I said, oh, Red Allen, a young fella. I said, he'd come up with him. He said, man, you mean to tell me this old man here come up under you? He was kidding him, you know? But he didn't look pretty old, though, you know? Yeah, I saw Red in Detroit. He and I and my wife and Hickam Bottom had a ball. Took him down to their hotel. Everything was on them. Perfect host. Wonderful, wonderful time. I'll never forget both of them. Well, the only time I had a deal with Hickam Bottom was in Kansas City, Missouri. He was with Duke Elton. Or Duke Armstrong or somebody. And I was there playing at a nightclub. In Kansas City? In Kansas City. Who was you playing with there? Well, I had the show band. The whole show, I had the band, Punch Miller. Yeah. But the whole show was there, the Browns Band again. Yeah, I see. And there's Wagon there in the nightclub. And all the band, Louie and all of them come on in. And Hickam Bottom come up and sit down and blow like they were. Oh, he was a hell of a... How about Louie Russell? Did you know Louie Russell? Piano player? Yeah. Man, sure. Did you ever make any records with him? Not with him. Did you ever play with him? Yeah, I said, I'm playing with him. Yeah. Was you in his band? No. You just sat in? Sit in. Just sit in.
Punch, in 1919, when you first got here, what did the brass bands play like? Were they strictly music? Were they here?

No, they played more marches then. But I'm going to tell you now, I ain't going to lie to you. Hick was a very few men's in them bands reading. Like the trumpet players be reading. But them other guys were just speaking. I mean, you know, using their brains. They could hear a tune and play it. That's right. Yeah. That's right. Now you take men like Joe Howard, and them men that were playing. They had their music up. They were playing it, see? But they had men on trombone, men on alto, and things like that. They had a good brain. They were following them. Can you read? Oh, yeah. How long have you been reading? See, I've been reading now about 12 years. 12 years. Then in these records that you made, you couldn't read? No. No. That's all up here. That's ideas that come at the time that you get up. That's right. You got the music all up here. You don't have to read, right? All right. Now, I'm going to tell you. I know the whole lot about music because I learned it from Mr. Joe Howard and a fellow named Paul Roger. I was going to tell you about music. But I'd get in bands like with Snagg Jones and all them kind of fellows playing by head. You didn't think about reading no music. We just go on and play something, see? Oh, yeah. The only band I sat down and read music with, best I could, was Tiny Pond and Jelly Roll Morton and Huey Swift. Them bands you had to put up on the front of you.
Well, what about Louie? Did you ever work with him?
Well, I didn't work with Louie no more than you had in New Orleans on parades and things.
Whose band would that be?
That was with the silver leaf. Frankie Dusen, I think, had the band.
Would Dusen be a reader? Not much.
Not much.
Was Louie reading then?

No. But what kind of brass band? Louie learned his reading from that woman he married, Lil. Lil Armstrong? Yeah, Louie got all his learning from Lil. About music, I'm telling you what I know. Well, now. But you got to give it to him. Louis was an apt fellow. Still apt. Heads, you know. Louis was so apt until if he, like, fellas now go to make a note and miss it, they might get mad and say, oh shucks or something like that. But Louis wouldn't. Louis would make a mistake on a horn and bust out and laugh and say, y'all, y'all watch me, see, I'm going to get it this time. I was kidding you that time. He learned all that weight, you see. Yeah. All that kind of stuff. Yeah. He was a good actor. He was a good showman. That's right. Sure. Let's see. How about Andy Kirk when you was in Kansas City? Did you ever set in with him or Benny Moten? I set in with Benny Moten. You never played with the band? Not study, no. How about McKinney's Cotton Pickers? Well, no. I never even set in with them, but I know them. You know them. Yeah. How about Noble Sissel? Noble Sissel, I work with him. We're rehearsing with him. You rehearsed with Noble Sissel, but you never played with him or anything? No. I tell you, a big humble come up with his band and two, three of the fellas fell out, not fell out, I mean got out the band and it seems like them was the various fellas he wanted and he just called it off. But we had been rehearsing about three or four days, see. Something was going on wrong, I didn't know what it was, but them fellas didn't show up on rehearsal. Did you ever meet Sidney DeParis? No, he didn't. Did you know Charlie Johnson? No. Did you ever play with Charlie Johnson? No, I never did play with Charlie Johnson. I'll tell you who I played with, Sidney's brother. Wilbur? Wilbur DeParis. You played with the band? He was in the band with me with the Miramac Miramakers, Wilbur Parrish on the trombone. What was the name of the band? Miramac Makers. Yeah, it was Miramac Makers.
Yeah, it was Miramac, you see, yeah.

Mac, Miramakers. Now this Mac, Mac and Mac. Yeah. But the name of the show was Miramac, Miramakers. Miramakers. They never made any records. Black but Sweet Old Gold. Alright, is Wilbur DeParis on that record? Yeah, he's on that record. Wilbur? Yeah. That's a guy. Let me tell you what he did. I made some kind of run on my trumpet, some kind of hell of a brick I made on my trumpet, and he went off somewhere and wrote it by music. And come back and said, Punch, can you play this? That's the truth of Miramac, I said, oh man, you know I can't play that. He said, well hell, you just made that on your own. I'll be damned. Now that's the truth. That's the truth of Miramac, I said, I said, I'm not going to play that. And I looked at him and I said, did I make that? He said, you shouldn't it in.
Who was the piano player with you?

Well, we had two, three, had a girl. That girl I told him about went nuts, Laura. Laura. Made her a long time. Then we had a fellow named Brownie, Clowns Brownie. Oh, two, three piano players. They didn't keep no good piano. Oh yeah, the boy died. James, James from Atlanta, Georgia. Johnson, James P. No, James, put James down, I'll call his name. He was a dope thing, he died. Not James, James, James from Atlanta, Georgia. Johnson, James P. No, James, put James down, I'll call his name. He was a dope thing till he died. Not James, I think that James Cadbury. Not James, see, James something.
Did Morris Rouse ever work with him? Who? Morris Rouse, Rouse, what can I pronounce it, Rouse or Rouse? Never knew him, huh?
Hemingway, James Hemingway. Hemingway. Yeah, James Hemingway. Now he was a good piano player.
Ever worked with Steve Lewis?
Well, I worked with Tranchinas with him.
Whose band was that?
Uh, uh, uh, Fate Marble. Not Fate Marble, I mean, P. Ron. A.J. P. Ron.
You worked with P. Ron, huh? Sure.

Did you ever, did you know Fate Marble? No. Did you ever play the riverboat? We were on the boat, from the other St. Louis. You played with Fate Marble on the riverboat. Yes, sir. Alright, now who else was in that group? Well, I know Fate was in it. See, every time I get into something like that, I'm in Lewis' place. Lewis had been on there with him. Yeah. And Lewis left. And I just got in there with him. You know, he only made one record. What is Fate? Yeah. Shall I? That's all he made, just one record. He was a piano man. I didn't make no record. Yeah, I know he was a piano man, but I didn't make no record with him. Alright, now who... Who was this big-eyed trumpet player he had? I don't know what his name is. I know he stood with Fate all the time. Lewis played with him and I played with him. That big brown skin fella, big poppy artist. I don't know what his name is.
I don't know what his name is.
That's not Norman Mason. Might be. Norman Mason's still out in St. Louis. Plays clarinet now.
Yeah, plays clarinet.
I've heard him, I know him. Well, that ain't him. This guy's a big trumpet player.
Well, Norman Mason used to be a trumpet player. Yeah.
He's a big fella? Not too big.
Amos White and Sidney Desvien on the record. What? Sidney Desvien and Amos White are on the record. That's bad.
Little of them.
No, that's in 24. They're on the record. I think it's 24.
When was you with Fate Marble on the boat? What year? About 21. 21? Yeah. Well, that's before the record. Yeah.
Back to those brass bands here. Well, the Silverleaf brass band, they wouldn't really be playing too much music then, huh? No. Well. They'd be faking a lot of it, huh? Yeah.

Silverleaf had some good musicians. Tuxedo had some good musicians. Now, you take, well, we'd call them the Zulu band. They had a hot brass band, see? Black Benny, myself, Lewis, and what does Tramon play our name? Eddie Morris. Not Eddie Morris. Morris. Morris. Morris French. Morris French played Tramon with Rene. Yeah. And all them kind of fellas. Well, they wasn't reading, but part of the day, they come down the street and tear the street up. Who's this Black Benny you're talking about? Well, he been dead a good while now, but he was a hell of a bass drum player. He was? A trap drummer too. He was a drummer then, huh? Yeah. What was his name? Benny what? Benny Williams. Benny Williams. They call him Black Benny though. Did you ever work with Chris Kelly's brass band? Not his brass band. I didn't have, Chris Kelly didn't have no brass band in the house. He had a jazz band. And you worked with him? Yeah. Played at the booths with him a lot of times. See, he had a stutter. You know, I had my band, but on Tuesday night I wouldn't be waking. Well, you know, that's how we used to do it. Were you playing Punch here when the Tenderloin was still in effect? still in effect? Tenderloin, what's that?
You mean the district?

The district. Oh hell yeah man. You was. I was playing with a fellow and Ken Beard in the daytime. Cans of the women, you know, the whole hustle of them. 10 cents a can and every night I'd get up there and play the blues with the piano player. Now he, I forget his name, he died. He was a sickly fellow but he died. But I, nothing but blues all night. I'd sit up and play the blues all night. A fellow named Tootlum. Tootlum. Gravity and Gravy. All right let me ask you this. It's known that Jelly Roll played here in the Tenderloins. Well let me tell you this. But there must have, did you ever hear of Tony Jackson? Yeah, whoever. I'm fixing to tell you now. I didn't know Jelly Roll here. You didn't? And I didn't know Tony Jackson here. Them fellow was gone I got here. King Oliver was gone. Johnny Dots was gone. I met them in Chicago. Freddy Keppert was gone. That's right. I worked with Freddy Keppert at the Dream Land. In Chicago? Did you work with Doc Cook? Yes sir. You worked with Doc Cook. That's right. That's right. That's sir.
Which band was it that Keppert was in you were in?
Keppert, he had his honor band then.
And you were with him huh?

Yeah. But Doc Cook played in the same place and I worked with him at the Dream Land. Well you know Keppert played with Cook and you played with Cook too. Yeah. Is that the same place? But I thought that was Fred's band. I didn't know no band. No, I didn't know. It was Cook's. Yes it was. Old Freddy Keppert was a fine fella boy. Drank pretty good didn't he? Oh he could drink some liquor. Did you drink very much when you was younger? Yeah I did a lot of drinking. Did you? Yeah but I tell you what happened with me. When I got to Chicago among all them kind of people I laid off liquor for a long time. You did? Yeah I got straight there but then they come to find that I was less of you too. But I stayed with him over two years. Yeah. Do you recall during these early days here in New Orleans some of the piano players that you knew? Well now I'm going to be straight Rich. In New Orleans back then in them early times we didn't never use a piano. You didn't? No sir. Never did. What did you use? Clannet, guitar, banjo, bass, violin, trumpet and drums. Yeah but all these whorehouses had pianos. Well the piano was by themselves mostly. They were? Yes sir. They never played with the group? No sir. Alright now would they have, would they have? I know there are plenty of piano players in them whorehouses. Who were some of them? Clowns, Todd. They had a sister named Camille Todd played in the sporting house. And they had a piano player, Tom Anderson. Tom Anderson? No he, that was a place. Yeah. Camilla. Camilla. But I think he did have a little band in there with his outfit. A little small band. Clarence Todd and Camilla Todd and who else? And uh, Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy Jimson or Jimmy Johnson or something. Jimmy Johnson? Yeah. James P? P John, but he had the band but he had a piano player there see. Well James P was a piano player. Well him, that's who he was. I didn't know. I didn't know.
Was this the guy from New York City? Yeah I think he was. Did you know him later in New York? I don't know.
I never seen him anymore but here.
Jimmy Johnson. What did he look like? What did he look like Jimmy? Well he was a dark slender fellow.

My boy, I can't help say about him for some reason cause he didn't ever do, he was a hell of a man but never made a record. Who's that? Buddy P. What did he play? Trumpet. Yeah. Nice trumpet player. Buddy never did. Did really ever make a record?
No. Rene did, yeah.
Yeah Rene did but not Buddy P.
Rene didn't make them until 1940 though.
He made those with Circles in there or something.
Well they were made for Bruin first on Delta. Yeah. But he was sharp they say compared to what he was earlier you see. That couldn't have been James P. Johnson. James P. Johnson was never skinny huh?
No I don't think so. I don't think so. Well his name was J, not JP but his name was Jimmy.
Jimmy.
Jimmy Johnson. Could that be two different people? Might be. Well they had two Jimmy Johnsons yeah.
I remember that. Did you know Burman have a black peep? Let's both play piano. No.
They might have played after I left. I mean.
No this was probably before you got in. The folks have really played the blues.
Well they had a lot of them blues played around here for her on piano.
I wonder what ever happened to Rappi?

This woman right down on this street. What street we on? St. Peter? Yeah right down there. She used to be a piano player in the nightclub. Larry know her name good. You know who I'm talking about. She lived 10, 1010 I believe. St. Peter. Johnson I think. Yeah well she used to play in the nightclub.
Cause I went there to get her one night for Larry. For Larry.

And she come on down and played some numbers. You know. Is any of these characters around that had these joints during that time? Is any of them still living? Who? Some of them some of the wives. Who?
Mrs. Tom Anderson is supposed to be alive.
Here in the city?
Have you ever. Well she would know nothing about it though.
She might. I want to know. Well Lula White died didn't she? Say Poncha.
Can y'all talk for a minute? Yeah.
Okay.
I got to go take a little beach.

So if he ain't got it now he'll never get it. That's for sure. And never forget I went to Memphis on an excursion from Chicago with a band. I had the band and they had five pieces. And a fella named Robert Henry had the outfit. And he asked each man in the band. He said uh now we're going in Memphis to a dance hall. And he said uh I think we're going to do good. He said now would y'all like to go in with the dance or just want a salary? And every one of them wanted a salary. They wanted twelve dollars a man for playing that night. He said well okay. So he said Poncha. He said well you just wake along with us. I said okay. I didn't care if I make a thing or not. I was drinking my liquor and doing a thing about it. And they had a great big yard full of something across the street before you get in the hall. All around the hall. And they're paying a dollar head at the gate. At the door. And did you know the yard was packed and jammed over seven hundred people and the hall was three hundred and something. About a dollar head. And he paid them all. And told him, now y'all got your own money. So now I got to do business with Poncha. I told you about that didn't you? Yeah. And I got five hundred and something out of it. Then I didn't get as much as I was supposed to get. But I got five hundred and about fifty dollars. Thank God. Oh my. For one night.
Well, how far away did you say they could hear you when you played trumpet and race last?
Bowie, Louisiana. One mile.
Mile, yeah.
A mile and a few, a little more than a mile.
And you also played at what, the National Park or Third and Wall? National Park, yeah.

You know all. That was Third and Willow. It's a school there now, big school. But it used to be a great big baseball park, see. And we didn't have nothing but a little shit over us. What did you play? Concerts or for dances? Dancers. For dances, huh? Yeah. She'd be loaded at them. Well, who would pay you for that? Well, Jack Kerry was doing it. See, he had the band. He was paying us nice, see. Shills, I, I, he wouldn't lie because he was so kind of dumb himself. And he couldn't do nothing but come clean, see. And he'd go to the gate and carry one of the boys with him and get the whole load of money. His little niece and her brother stood at the gate. She collected money, dialed six pieces of paper a piece. Come in, you know, come in. And he'd bring that whole load of money there and put it around the bandstand and say, y'all come up in the county. And we counted out of them. Take our parts. Sometimes, you know, in them days, $15, hell. In them days, sometimes we'd get $15 a piece out of it. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, how far away could they hear you when you were at 3rd and Willow?
I'm telling you, they hear them at Rampart and Junior? That's a good raise, man.
Speaking of Rampart and Junior, why don't we put something about how you got sick on the tape, huh? Hmm? Let's put something on the tape about how you got sick.

Well, I'll tell you about that. The same little show I was been to called the Browns Mannequins. That had been a few years back. Now more than, I'd been more than 12 years. I had ate a piece of some rice pudding in Pensacola, Florida. I was going from Pensacola to Nashville. It was a good gym, see? And just on halfway, that rice custard got under your boy and I couldn't get no breath and nothing. Oh, it was giving me a fit. So they took me to the hospital in Nashville. They rushed me to the hospital. And a little young doctor, if I'd have listened at him, I'd have been a good man today. He told me, but I just thought he was too young. He said, you know what? I said, what? He said, the rice custard's not doing you all that bad. He said, but you got a gallstone coming and someday you got to be out reeling if I was you, I would do it right now while you're in the hospital and get it over with. So I tell him, I said, well, if it's coming, I said, I'll just wait a few days and find out. Then if it's getting bad, I'll come back. But I never did go back. And the gallstones kept getting bigger and bigger and bigger and bigger. And then it really comes to going down, see? Going down. Year by year, I was going down. So I got so bad, that's how you had to pick me up and take me home to the hospital. Didn't you ever connect the two punch at that time? When you started feeling so bad, didn't you ever think about what this doctor told you? I thought about it a lot of times. Didn't do nothing about it? I was scared of a knife. That's my trouble. That's my only trouble. And I wouldn't have went under the knife this time, but I just could not help it. I just had to go. But I was always scared of operation. Why? I don't know why. You're not afraid to die, are you? Well, to tell the truth, I am, yeah, but I've got to die. You are. Yeah. When the time comes, you won't think a bit more of it and you're sitting here talking to me.
Well, I've got something to know. How do you know?

Because I've been almost dead twice. And it don't bother you a bit. Well, punch, I thought you had cancer when I came up to the hotel. No. That's what the doctor, we were worried that you had cancer, so we rushed you into charity. No, gallstone.
Well, I know. We know that now, but we didn't know that then. Well, I know that then.
I know that then.
I know that then. I know that then. I know that I had a gallstone. And they tried to give me medicine to pass it out, you know?

Well, I wouldn't say they're trying to give me medicine to pass it out, because the doctors were taking extra of me every day and they couldn't find out what we were on. Took me all kind of ways, couldn't find me. They did find out they laid about six or four little pillars, you know? And told me they lay with my back right on them. They took x-ray from the side. They took x-ray from the side. They found out under the liver, the gallstone was under my liver. Oh. It was under there. Oh. And they said I had a pretty dangerous escape there. They had to get under there and cut some of my liver to get to the gallstone. Well, how are you feeling now? Oh, I feel good there now. Other than the high blood pressure now, you're in good shape. Yes, I am. And you're still blowing. You're practicing every other day? Pretty much every day I practice. Do you think that you'll be playing again? The way I feel, I would. The other two Sundays ago, they had a parade way up there, and Adam, in the saloon. And the boys was in there playing. And for some reason, I seen a trumpet laying on the table, you know? And I just couldn't resist. I picked up the trumpet and went to blowing. Everybody started to holler. You blow good? Sure. That's right.
I was there, but I didn't know it was you. You was there?
Well, I sure did blow.
There was some crowd. Yeah.

I blowed like a dog in there, man. Yes, of them. How long did you play? Oh, I must have played about half an hour or more. Is that right? I played about four different tunes. Did you feel any ill effects? Tell me one thing I felt a little dizzy after. I did, I ain't kidding, but they said that's my blood. Yeah. So that's what I got to watch. But down here, nothing. No. Do you eat good? Yeah, I eat heavy. Can you eat anything? No, I have to. You have to watch your diet. Yeah. I see. Yeah, I watch my diet. I don't bother with no kind of salt, no kind of pork. Very little such thing as starch food. You're not ready. When I fix a hamburger, I taste water and put it in the skillet and a little piece of butter and put a lid over it.
Yeah, well you got to watch that diabetes too, you see.

Well, I don't have no trouble with that. I just care of that. You know what I mean? I don't have no trouble with that. Of course, it's dangerous, but I don't have no trouble with it. Yeah, well. Because I've been taking care of it way before I got high up here. Yeah, way before I went to the hospital and I don't have time. Yeah.

segments.title: Opening: recording date and playing Punch his records
segments.summary: Dick Allen announces the date and place, 1 Sept 1959 on St. Peter Street, and says they will play Punch his records to identify them.

segments.title: Sir Oliver Bibbs, drummer and bandleader in Chicago
segments.summary: Punch recalls working with drummer Sir Oliver Bibbs at Chicago clubs and in Springfield; Allen asks about his leaving Chicago.

segments.title: Boyhood friends and nicknames while listening to records
segments.summary: Punch names boyhood friends from the country, such as Johnny 'Rooster' Johnson, while a record plays.

segments.title: Playing guitar-and-horn duets with Lonnie Johnson in Raceland
segments.summary: Punch says he and Lonnie played as boys near Raceland for about three years, doing blues and old numbers.

segments.title: Blind Willie Dunn records and seeing Lonnie Johnson in Cleveland
segments.summary: Discussion of Lonnie Johnson on Blind Willie Dunn records and whether King Oliver played; Punch saw Lonnie do a guitar act with a show in Cleveland.

segments.title: Joe Howard, the trumpeter who taught Punch
segments.summary: Punch says Joe Howard showed him a lot on trumpet before he left New Orleans, and learns Howard has died.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: Red Allen, Higginbotham and Luis Russell
segments.summary: Punch says he never played with Henry or Red Allen but taught Red, tells of Higginbotham in Kansas City, and sat in with Luis Russell.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: Brass bands in 1919 and who read music
segments.summary: Punch explains that the brass bands played marches by ear with few readers, and that he learned music from Joe Howard and Paul Roger.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: Louis Armstrong: parades, Lil's teaching, and sitting in with Kansas City bands
segments.summary: Punch says he only worked with Louis on parades in New Orleans, with the Silver Leaf band under Frankie Dusen, where reading was not much required. One long answer: Louis learned reading from Lil and laughed at mistakes; Punch sat in with Moten, rehearsed with Noble Sissle, and played with Wilbur DeParis in the Miramac Makers.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: The Miramac Makers show and Wilbur DeParis
segments.summary: Punch describes the Miramac Makers show, never recorded, and Wilbur DeParis writing out a run Punch had improvised.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: Piano players in the Miramac band
segments.summary: Punch struggles to name the band's several pianists and recalls James Hemingway as a good one.

segments.chapter: Musicians he knew and played with
segments.title: Fate Marble's riverboat band and Steve Lewis
segments.summary: Punch says he took Steve Lewis's place in Fate Marble's band on the riverboats around 1921; they try to identify the big trumpeter in the band.

segments.title: Silver Leaf, Tuxedo and Zulu brass bands, Black Benny and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Punch describes the hot Zulu brass band with Black Benny, and playing with Chris Kelly's jazz band.

segments.title: The Tenderloin district and Freddie Keppard at the Dreamland
segments.summary: Punch played blues in the district; he did not know Jelly Roll, Tony Jackson or Oliver there but worked with Keppard and Doc Cook in Chicago.

segments.title: Doc Cook, drinking, and sporting-house pianists such as Jimmy Johnson
segments.summary: Punch talks about drinking, says early New Orleans bands used no piano, and recalls pianists like the Todds and a Jimmy Johnson.

segments.title: Blues pianists and surviving figures from the district
segments.summary: Allen and Punch discuss blues piano players, a woman pianist on St. Peter, and whether Mrs. Tom Anderson is alive, before a break.

segments.chapter: Money, touring and the loud horn
segments.title: Memphis excursion dance that paid Punch five hundred dollars
segments.summary: Punch tells how he took a share of the gate instead of salary for a Memphis dance and made about $550.

segments.chapter: Money, touring and the loud horn
segments.title: How far Punch's trumpet carried and dances at National Park
segments.summary: Punch says his horn could be heard a mile, and describes playing for dances at National Park under Jack Carey for about $15 each.

segments.title: Gallstone illness that began on tour in Pensacola
segments.summary: Punch tells of rice pudding in Pensacola, a doctor's warning about gallstones, his fear of surgery, and the hospital stay.

segments.title: Recovery, diet and blowing trumpet again
segments.summary: Punch describes the surgery, his health, daily practice, sitting in on trumpet recently and his diet.
